title: IAT New Test 11
review_status: fresh AI-assisted authoring; independent academic review pending
notification_source: Official IAT 2026 examination page and 2026 Information Brochure, sections 19 and 23; a 2027 brochure has not been verified
past_paper_reference: 539 English archive entries from 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2021–2026; 2026 key provisional; analysed for topic/style only, no questions copied
authoring_source: Individually authored TSV records against the 25-test slot plan; mechanical assembly only; academic review pending
order_policy: fixed authored order; do not shuffle questions or options or renumber image-linked IDs
instructions: This is an original preparation pilot for manual review, based on the verified 2026 scheme; it is not an official IAT paper or a verified 2027 notification.
There are 60 single-correct questions: Biology 1–15, Chemistry 16–30, Mathematics 31–45 and Physics 46–60.
Each question has exactly one correct option. Correct: +4; incorrect: -1; unanswered: 0. All questions are available to attempt; there is no best-three-subject scoring rule.
Use 180 minutes. An on-screen non-programmable scientific calculator is part of the 2026 examination conditions; personal calculators are not allowed under that scheme.
Treat stated data and idealisations as exact unless an approximation is explicitly supplied. Log denotes base 10 and ln denotes the natural logarithm.
The review PDF contains the question paper first, followed by a separate answer key and worked solutions. Keep the solutions hidden during a timed attempt.

difficulty_policy.basis: user-directed editorial mix, not measured item difficulty

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The seed-section figure shows an embryo enclosed by a seed coat and a fruit wall derived from the ovary. Which inference is best supported?
options: A) The plant must be a gymnosperm
B) The ovule was enclosed in an ovary before fruit development
C) The seed contains no embryo
D) The fruit wall formed from the pollen grain
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) An enclosed ovule.
Why: An angiosperm's ovary encloses ovules and later contributes the fruit wall; an ovule matures into a seed. Seeing both outer fruit wall and internal seed supports this developmental route, not a classification by seed number alone.
Why not the others: (A) gymnosperm seeds lack an enclosing ovary-derived fruit; (C) contradicts the pictured embryo; (D) pollen contributes male gametes rather than fruit wall.
Key point: Trace ovule and ovary into different mature structures.
questions.image_alt: Fruit wall enclosing seed and embryo

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: Use the root cross-section in the figure. Which identification and vascular arrangement fit?
options: A) Monocot root with many radial xylem poles
B) Dicot stem with scattered bundles
C) Dicot root with radial xylem and phloem
D) Monocot stem with closed collateral bundles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Dicot root.
Why: Radial separation of xylem and phloem plus star-shaped central xylem and small pith is characteristic of a young dicot root. It is anatomical evidence about vascular arrangement, not a statement that water and food move in the same cells.
Why not the others: (A) monocot roots usually have many poles and larger pith; (B) stems arrange bundles differently; (D) scattered closed bundles describe a monocot stem.
Key point: Combine stele arrangement and pith before assigning organ type.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two glucose residues join by a covalent bond after removal of one H₂O molecule. Which linkage type is formed in a disaccharide?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Glycosidic bond.
Why: Condensation between hydroxyl groups on monosaccharides joins them through an oxygen bridge, a glycosidic linkage, while releasing water. The precise anomeric configuration requires structure information beyond this description.
Why not the others: (A) joins amino-acid residues; (B) links nucleotides in a sugar-phosphate backbone; (C) is a different carboxylic-acid/alcohol linkage.
Key point: Identify the constituent monomers before naming their bond.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two leaves at the same light and temperature have equal stomatal aperture. Leaf X is in dry air; Y is in humid air. X loses more water while short-term CO₂ uptake is similar. Which mechanism best explains the divergence?
options: A) Steeper water-vapour gradient drives greater transpiration from X
B) Dry air makes the stomatal pore physically wider despite the stated equality
C) Humid air abolishes photosynthesis entirely
D) Water moves from air into X because its vapour pressure is lower
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Steeper vapour gradient.
Why: Equal apertures control stomatal conductance approximately, but dry outside air lowers external water-vapour partial pressure, steepening the outward diffusion gradient. CO₂ uptake may remain similar if internal carbon supply and other limitations compensate; a short observation does not prove identical total photosynthesis.
Why not the others: (B) violates the controlled aperture observation; (C) is unsupported by measured uptake; (D) reverses the stated net water loss direction.
Key point: Separate conductance from the driving partial-pressure difference.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: At an active tissue, CO₂ rises and pH falls while the incoming arterial blood is unchanged. What effect on haemoglobin helps deliver more O₂ locally?
options: A) A left shift and stronger O₂ binding
B) A right shift and lower O₂ affinity
C) No change because blood pH cannot vary
D) Conversion of O₂ into CO₂ inside haemoglobin
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Right shift.
Why: Higher CO₂ and H⁺ favour haemoglobin conformations with lower oxygen affinity (Bohr effect). At the same tissue oxygen partial pressure, a right-shifted dissociation curve allows more oxygen unloading.
Why not the others: (A) would hinder unloading; (C) ignores local acidification; (D) confuses gas transport and chemical conversion.
Key point: Compare affinity at fixed local oxygen pressure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A self-pollinated flower receives viable pollen that germinates on its stigma but its tube stops in the style; unrelated pollen reaches the ovule and seeds form. What mechanism best fits the control?
options: B) Absence of any functional ovule
C) Self-incompatibility rejecting self pollen after germination
D) Mechanical absence of a stigma
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Self-incompatibility.
Why: The viable self pollen starts germination but fails later, whereas unrelated pollen travels through the same style and produces seeds. This bypass comparison localises rejection to recognition or growth after contact, rather than a general defect in the female tract.
Why not the others: (A) self pollen was present and viable; (B) cross-pollination produced seeds; (D) pollen germinated on the stigma.
Key point: A compatible cross controls for general floral viability.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two equally large isolated populations each follow Hardy–Weinberg proportions: their A-allele frequencies are 0.8 and 0.2. They are pooled for sampling before any cross-population mating. How does the pooled heterozygote fraction compare with the Hardy–Weinberg expectation calculated from pooled p=0.5?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Observed 0.32 versus expected 0.50.
Given: Each population has 2pq=2(0.8)(0.2)=0.32 heterozygotes; equal weighting preserves 0.32 in the pooled sample.
Formula/Principle: The pooled allele frequency is 0.5, whose random-mating expectation would be 2(0.5)(0.5)=0.50.
Step 1: Population structure without interbreeding causes a heterozygote deficit relative to a single randomly mating population.
Why: Hardy–Weinberg genotype frequencies require random mating within the population considered. Combining two internally random-mating groups with different allele frequencies before cross-mating does not create the heterozygotes predicted by pooled allele frequency. This is a structure effect, not evidence that an allele changed.
Why not the others: (A) assumes pooled random mating already occurred; (B) overcounts heterozygotes; (C) confuses an allele frequency or homozygote share with heterozygote fraction.
Key point: Check the population boundary before applying 2pq.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the fermentation figure, identify microbes P and Q from their observed products. Which pair is consistent?
options: A) P is yeast; Q is Lactobacillus
B) P is Lactobacillus; Q is yeast
D) P is a virus; Q is a cyanobacterium
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Yeast and Lactobacillus.
Why: Yeast fermentation produces CO₂ that leavens dough and ethanol, while lactic-acid bacteria convert milk sugars to lactic acid and lower curd pH. The paired product evidence distinguishes both organisms better than a single habitat clue.
Why not the others: (B) reverses the characteristic fermentations; (C) methanogens produce methane under different conditions; (D) neither proposed organism matches both food processes.
Key point: Match microbes to products and substrate context.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The figure shows a vector opened with two different restriction enzymes, E and H, and an insert prepared with matching E and H ends. Their sticky overhang sequences are noncompatible with one another. Why is insertion favoured in one orientation?
options: A) Both ends are identical, so either orientation works
B) Each insert end can anneal only to its corresponding vector end, then ligase seals the aligned backbone
C) The E end can ligate to both E and H sites equally
D) The insert has no phosphates, so orientation is irrelevant
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Distinct compatible end pairs enforce orientation.
Why: The E overhang of insert pairs with vector E, and H pairs with H; swapping the insert would place noncomplementary E opposite H at both junctions. Complementary annealing establishes the allowed geometry, then ligase closes phosphodiester bonds. This reduces reverse insertion and simple self-ligation relative to using one identical site, although experimental verification remains necessary.
Why not the others: (A) contradicts the nonidentical ends; (C) ignores sequence-specific pairing; (D) a phosphate backbone is required for covalent sealing and does not remove orientation constraints.
Key point: Two different noncompatible overhangs give directional cloning.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A population grows by 20% annually at low density, but in later years additions diminish as size nears a stable level while births continue. Which description fits the later regime?
options: A) Constant exponential growth with unlimited resources
C) Density-limited approach to carrying capacity
D) A fixed annual decrease regardless of density
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Density limitation.
Why: Slowing increments near a stable size imply per-capita net growth declines as density increases and limiting resources or interactions become important. Births can continue while balanced by mortality; a plateau does not mean reproduction stops.
Why not the others: (A) would retain proportional growth; (B) contradicts stable persistence; (D) predicts falling numbers rather than diminishing increments.
Key point: Compare per-capita growth across density levels.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A pesticide-resistance allele is rare before spraying. After repeated exposure, resistant insects survive and leave more offspring, and the allele frequency rises. Which process is directly illustrated?
options: A) Directed mutation induced in every insect by need
B) Random drift without differential survival
C) Acquired resistance inherited because individual insects practised tolerance
D) Natural selection acting on heritable variation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Natural selection.
Why: A pre-existing heritable variant becomes common when the environment changes relative survival and reproduction. The frequency trend and survival comparison support selection; they do not show that pesticide intentionally created an allele.
Why not the others: (A) asserts need-directed mutation; (B) ignores differential fitness; (C) invokes inheritance of acquired training.
Key point: Selection changes variant frequency through unequal reproductive success.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two independent genes A/a and B/b affect a visible trait. An AaBb individual is test-crossed with aabb. If segregation and assortment are independent, what fraction of offspring are AaBb?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) One quarter.
Given: AaBb produces AB,Ab,aB,ab gametes equally; aabb produces ab only.
Formula/Principle: P(AB gamete)=P(A)P(B)=(1/2)(1/2).
Step 1: AB×ab produces AaBb in 1/4 of offspring.
Why: The recessive tester exposes each gamete from the heterozygote directly in offspring genotype. Independent assortment is the reason the two halves multiply; linkage would alter this prediction.
Why not the others: (B) counts only one locus; (C) counts any heterozygosity; (D) treats every gamete as AB.
Key point: Decode a two-locus test cross by gamete types.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A substance is filtered into a nephron at 100 mg min⁻¹, is neither secreted nor metabolised, and appears in urine at 25 mg min⁻¹. How much is reabsorbed per minute?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 75 mg min⁻¹.
Given: Filtered 100 mg min⁻¹; excreted 25 mg min⁻¹; secretion zero.
Formula/Principle: Excretion=filtration−reabsorption+secretion.
Step 1: Reabsorption=100−25=75 mg min⁻¹.
Why: No secretion or metabolism occurs. Thus, the missing filtered material must return to blood, so the reabsorbed amount is determined. The 25 mg/min appearing in urine is the residual after this return from the filtered load.
Why not the others: (A) repeats excretion; (C) assumes no urine loss; (D) adds rather than subtracts.
Key point: Use a mass balance with all transport routes stated.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Membrane vesicles accumulate glucose uphill only when an outward Na⁺ gradient is established; ATP is absent, and collapse of the Na⁺ gradient stops uptake. Which mechanism is supported?
options: A) Passive diffusion of glucose alone
B) Primary glucose ATPase directly hydrolysing ATP
C) Secondary active co-transport using Na⁺ gradient
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Secondary active transport.
Why: Glucose moves against its own concentration gradient, requiring coupled free energy. The independently imposed sodium gradient drives the uphill uptake through a co-transporter even without ATP in the vesicle assay.
Why not the others: (A) cannot explain uphill transport; (B) contradicts ATP absence; (D) is not uptake from outside.
Key point: An ion gradient can power another molecule's uphill transport.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: In a young dicot stem, a cambial ring forms from vascular-cambium strips within bundles and tissue between bundles. What is the origin of that tissue between bundles?
options: A) Dead vessel elements in xylem
D) Interfascicular parenchyma that becomes meristematic
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Interfascicular parenchyma.
Why: Parenchyma between vascular bundles can regain meristematic activity, linking the intrafascicular cambial segments into a continuous ring. That ring produces secondary vascular tissues; the question asks its origin, not the final products.
Why not the others: (A) differentiated dead xylem cannot divide; (B) is an external protective layer; (C) is leaf photosynthetic tissue.
Key point: Distinguish cambium formed inside and between stem bundles.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which proposed resonance contributor for the carbonate ion CO₃²⁻ is valid under the usual octet Lewis description?
options: A) One C=O and two C–O⁻ bonds, carbon with eight electrons
B) Three C=O double bonds at one carbon
C) One C–O bond and two unbonded oxygen atoms
D) A carbonate contributor with a carbon radical
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) One double and two single bonds.
Why: Carbon's octet accommodates one double bond and two single bonds to oxygen. Two singly bonded oxygens each carry formal charge −1; alternative equivalent contributors put the double bond at another oxygen without moving nuclei.
Why not the others: (B) puts twelve bonding electrons around second-period C; (C) loses the three connected C–O bonds; (D) invents an unpaired electron absent from the ion.
Key point: Resonance moves electrons, not atoms, and obeys octets.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure shows ionisation isomers X and Y. Their aqueous samples receive BaCl₂ separately. Which sample yields immediate BaSO₄ from a free counter-ion?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Only X.
Why: Sulfate lies outside the coordination sphere of X as an exchangeable counter-ion, so Ba²⁺ precipitates it. In Y sulfate is coordinated and bromide is the free counter-ion; the immediate sulfate test distinguishes ionisation isomers without requiring dissociation of the complex.
Why not the others: (A) reverses inner and outer sphere; (C) treats coordinated sulfate as free; (D) ignores X's counter-ion.
Key point: Locate the ion outside square brackets before predicting a rapid wet test.
questions.image_alt: Ionisation isomers and sulfate wet-test observations

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Across the lanthanoid series, the ionic radii of common Ln³⁺ ions generally decrease. What causes this trend?
options: C) Weak shielding by added 4f electrons as nuclear charge increases
D) Elimination of all inner-shell electrons
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Weak 4f shielding.
Why: Additional protons attract the electron cloud more strongly, while added 4f electrons incompletely screen that charge from outer electrons. The resulting effective nuclear-charge rise contracts successive trivalent ions.
Why not the others: (A) misidentifies the subshell filled; (B) nuclear charge increases; (D) inner shells remain occupied.
Key point: Compare increasing nuclear charge with incomplete 4f screening.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question: Among O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺, all with ten electrons, which ion has the smallest radius?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Mg²⁺.
Why: Isoelectronic ions have the same electron count but different proton counts. Mg²⁺ has the largest nuclear charge among the four, so it attracts the common ten-electron cloud most strongly, producing the smallest radius.
Why not the others: (A) has only eight protons; (B) nine; (C) eleven versus magnesium's twelve.
Key point: Within an isoelectronic series, radius decreases with nuclear charge.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: For hydrogen, what is the limiting photon energy of the Balmer series as the upper level n approaches infinity? Use Eₙ=−13.6/n² eV.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3.4 eV.
Given: Balmer transitions terminate at n=2.
Formula/Principle: Photon energy=13.6(1/2²−1/n²) eV.
Step 1: As n→∞, second term tends to zero, giving 13.6/4=3.4 eV.
Why: The series limit corresponds to excitation from n=2 to the continuum, not from the ground state. The photon energy approaches a finite maximum even though the upper quantum number is unbounded.
Why not the others: (B) is the ground-state ionisation energy; (C) is a finite Balmer gap; (D) is the first Lyman gap.
Key point: Identify the series' fixed lower level first.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A 250 mL sample of 0.40 M acid HA is diluted to 500 mL. A 100 mL aliquot of the diluted acid reacts 1:1 with NaOH. How many moles of NaOH are needed for complete neutralisation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.020 mol.
Given: Initial acid 0.250×0.40=0.100 mol; dilution gives 0.20 M.
Formula/Principle: Aliquot acid moles=0.100 L×0.20 M; neutralisation ratio 1:1.
Step 1: 0.020 mol HA in aliquot, hence 0.020 mol NaOH.
Why: Dilution leaves the whole batch's acid moles unchanged but spreads them over twice the volume. Only one fifth of the final batch is titrated, so using all 0.100 mol would overcount.
Why not the others: (A) halves the aliquot amount again; (C) uses undiluted concentration; (D) treats the entire batch as the aliquot.
Key point: Recalculate concentration, then use aliquot volume.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Follow the electron-flow arrows in the carbonyl addition figure. Which role does CN⁻ play in the bond-forming step?
options: A) Electrophile accepting an electron pair
B) Leaving group departing from a saturated carbon
C) Nucleophile donating a pair to an electrophilic carbon
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Nucleophile.
Why: The carbonyl bond is polarised toward oxygen, leaving carbon electron-deficient. Cyanide supplies an electron pair to form a new C–C bond while π electrons move to oxygen, the defining electron-flow pattern for nucleophilic addition.
Why not the others: (A) reverses electron-pair flow; (B) no departure is shown; (D) CN⁻ does not donate a proton here.
Key point: Follow curved-arrow electron donation, not reagent charge alone.
questions.image_alt: Carbonyl addition arrow and cyanide pair

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A ring has CH₃ at carbon 1 and Br at carbon 4. Under mild nitration, both groups direct ortho/para but they favour different available positions. Which site is favoured mainly by the more activating group, assuming steric effects do not reverse the directing effect?
options: A) Carbon 4 already occupied by Br
B) Carbon 3 or 5, meta to CH₃
C) Carbon 1 already occupied by CH₃
D) Carbon 2 or 6, ortho to CH₃
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Carbon 2 or 6.
Why: Methyl is activating and ortho/para directing; at a para-bromotoluene framework its para site is occupied, so the equivalent positions 2 and 6 are available. Bromine also directs ortho/para but deactivates the ring, making its preference at positions 3/5 less influential under the stated comparison.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are already substituted sites; (B) follows bromine's direction while ignoring stronger methyl activation.
Key point: Resolve competing directing effects using relative activation and occupancy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Under ordinary SN2 conditions with aqueous hydroxide, why does bromobenzene react much more slowly than bromoethane?
options: A) Bromobenzene's C–Br bond is to an sp² carbon and resists backside substitution
B) Bromobenzene contains no polar bond
C) Bromoethane has an aromatic ring
D) Bromobenzene has a more accessible tetrahedral reaction centre
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Aryl sp² carbon resists SN2.
Why: SN2 requires backside approach to a tetrahedral carbon; the aromatic sp² carbon and C–Br bond with partial double-bond character obstruct that path. The ordinary primary alkyl bromide offers an accessible saturated centre for displacement.
Why not the others: (B) the aryl C–Br bond is polar; (C) bromoethane is aliphatic; (D) reverses the structural comparison.
Key point: Match the reaction mechanism to the carbon bearing the leaving group.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Anisole (Ph–O–CH₃) is treated with excess concentrated HI under ether-cleavage conditions. Which main pair of products reflects cleavage at the alkyl side?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Phenol and CH₃I.
Why: Protonation of the ether oxygen makes cleavage easier; iodide attacks the methyl carbon through an accessible SN2 path. The aryl C–O bond is not cleaved by ordinary backside attack on sp² carbon, leaving phenol.
Why not the others: (A) requires aryl substitution and the wrong alcohol; (C) lacks the iodide product; (D) changes oxygen to nitrogen without a source.
Key point: Unsymmetrical aryl–alkyl ethers cleave at the alkyl carbon.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Sucrose solution gives a negative Benedict test before hydrolysis but becomes positive after complete acid hydrolysis followed by neutralisation. What accounts for the change?
options: A) Sucrose is initially an aldehyde that acid removes
B) Hydrolysis converts both monomers to non-sugars
C) Hydrolysis releases reducing monosaccharides with available anomeric centres
D) Benedict reagent directly hydrolyses sucrose
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Reducing products after hydrolysis.
Why: Sucrose links both anomeric carbons, preventing the free hemiacetal/hemiketal forms needed for reduction in the initial assay. Hydrolysis liberates glucose and fructose, which can participate in reducing-sugar chemistry under the alkaline test conditions.
Why not the others: (A) sucrose is initially nonreducing; (B) products remain sugars; (D) the stipulated acid hydrolysis occurs before the neutralised test.
Key point: Check whether anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A monoprotic weak acid has analytical concentration 0.10 M and measured equilibrium [H⁺]=1.0×10⁻³ M in water, with water autoionisation negligible. What is Ka?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) About 1.01×10⁻⁵.
Given: [A⁻]=x=0.001 M, [HA]=0.10−x=0.099 M.
Formula/Principle: Ka=x²/(C−x).
Step 1: 10⁻⁶/0.099≈1.0101×10⁻⁵.
Why: The measured hydrogen concentration equals the dissociation extent for the specified monoprotic acid. Keeping the small depletion in the denominator provides the stated precise value rather than just an order-of-magnitude approximation.
Why not the others: (A) reports x; (B) moves the decimal place one too far; (C) omits the denominator.
Key point: Use equilibrium concentrations rather than analytical concentration blindly.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: From the freezing-point graph for a 0.10 m electrolyte A₂B solution and the displayed solvent constant, estimate its degree of dissociation into three ions.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) About 0.63.
Given: ΔTf=0.42 K, Kf=1.86, m=0.10; complete dissociation would produce three ions.
Formula/Principle: i=ΔTf/(Kfm)=1+2α for A₂B→2A+B.
Step 1: i=0.42/0.186≈2.258; α=(i−1)/2≈0.629.
Why: The observed depression exceeds the non-electrolyte value but is below the three-particle full-dissociation limit. Each dissociated formula unit adds two net particles relative to one undissociated unit.
Why not the others: (B) treats i−1 as a different ion count; (C) copies ΔT; (D) takes i−1 without dividing by two and exceeds unity.
Key point: Infer particle factor before converting it into dissociation fraction.
questions.image_alt: Freezing point difference and solvent constant

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: An aqueous CuSO₄ cell with inert electrodes is electrolysed so that 0.020 mol electrons pass. Assuming Cu²⁺ plates at the cathode and water oxidises to O₂ at the anode, what are the product amounts?
options: A) 0.020 mol Cu and 0.020 mol O₂
B) 0.010 mol Cu and 0.005 mol O₂
C) 0.040 mol Cu and 0.010 mol O₂
D) 0.005 mol Cu and 0.010 mol O₂
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.010 mol Cu, 0.005 mol O₂.
Given: 0.020 mol electrons; Cu²⁺+2e⁻→Cu, and water oxidation releases one O₂ per four electrons.
Formula/Principle: Product moles=electron moles divided by electrons per product.
Step 1: Cu=0.020/2=0.010 mol; O₂=0.020/4=0.005 mol.
Why: Cathode and anode consume or release the same charge but have distinct electron stoichiometries. Assuming inert electrodes avoids metal-anode dissolution, which would change the products.
Why not the others: (A) uses one electron per product; (C) multiplies instead of divides for Cu; (D) exchanges the two denominators.
Key point: Balance both electrode half reactions separately.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Use ΔHf° (kJ mol⁻¹): CH₄(g)=−75, CO₂(g)=−394, H₂O(l)=−286, O₂(g)=0. What is ΔH° for CH₄+2O₂→CO₂+2H₂O(l)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −891 kJ mol⁻¹.
Given: Formation enthalpies for products and reactants.
Formula/Principle: ΔHrxn=ΣνΔHf(products)−ΣνΔHf(reactants).
Step 1: [−394+2(−286)]−[−75+0]=−966+75=−891.
Why: Hess's law combines state-function formation enthalpies with balanced stoichiometric coefficients. Including the physical state of water matters because liquid and vapour have different formation values.
Why not the others: (A) omits water or methane contributions; (B) reverses sign; (D) uses an incorrect product sum.
Key point: Multiply each formation value by its reaction coefficient.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For the ellipse x²/16+y²/12=1, what are its eccentricity and the positive x-directrix coordinate?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1/2 and x=8.
Given: a²=16, b²=12 for major axis x.
Formula/Principle: c²=a²−b²; e=c/a; directrix x=a/e.
Step 1: c=2, a=4, e=1/2, x=8.
Worked derivation: \[c=\sqrt{16-12}=2,\quad e=\frac24=\frac12,\quad x_{\rm directrix}=\frac a e=8.\]
Why: The focus distance is not itself eccentricity; it must be normalised by the semimajor axis. The positive directrix lies outside the right vertex x=4.
Why not the others: (A) divides twice; (B) uses the vertex as directrix; (C) confuses b/a with eccentricity.
Key point: Compute c, then e, then the directrix.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Find the slope of the tangent to x²+xy+y²=7 at (1,2).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) −4/5.
Given: (1,2) lies on the curve because 1+2+4=7.
Formula/Principle: Implicitly differentiate both x and y terms.
Step 1: 2x+y+xy′+2yy′=0.
Worked derivation: \[y'=-\frac{2x+y}{x+2y},\quad y'(1,2)=-\frac{2+2}{1+4}=-\frac45.\]
Why: The xy term has both a direct x derivative and a y′ term. Treating y as constant when differentiating it would lose the denominator contribution.
Why not the others: (B) inverts rise/run; (C) loses minus sign; (D) omits the xy product derivative.
Key point: Include y′ whenever a factor y depends on x.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: What is the finite area enclosed by y=x² and y=2x−x²?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/3.
Given: Intersections satisfy x²=2x−x².
Formula/Principle: Area=∫(upper−lower) dx between crossings.
Step 1: 2x(x−1)=0 gives x=0,1; upper is 2x−x² between them.
Worked derivation: \[A=\int_0^1[(2x-x^2)-x^2]dx=\int_0^1(2x-2x^2)dx=\left[x^2-\frac23x^3\right]_0^1=\frac13.\]
Why: Both curves share the crossing endpoints, and the linear-minus-quadratic curve is above in between. Integrating only one curve or reversing their order changes the enclosed area.
Why not the others: (A) halves the difference; (C) doubles the area; (D) uses a bounding rectangle.
Key point: Solve intersections and decide vertical order before integration.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Consider f: ℝ→[0,∞) defined by f(x)=x². Which classification is correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Onto, not one-to-one.
Worked derivation: \[f(a)=f(-a)\ (a\ne0),\qquad \forall y\ge0,\ f(\sqrt y)=y.\]
Why: Opposite nonzero inputs collide, so injection fails. Every nonnegative codomain value has a real preimage, including zero, so the function is surjective onto the expressly stated codomain.
Why not the others: (A) reverses both properties; (B) overlooks ±a; (D) treats the codomain as all reals.
Key point: Onto depends on the specified codomain.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For a 3×3 matrix A with det A=−2, what is tr(A adj A)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) −6.
Given: A is 3×3 and detA=−2.
Formula/Principle: A adj A=(det A)I₃.
Step 1: Trace of −2I₃ is three times −2.
Worked derivation: \[\operatorname{tr}(A\operatorname{adj}A)=\operatorname{tr}[-2I_3]=-2\cdot3=-6.\]
Why: The adjugate identity converts the whole matrix product to a scalar multiple of the identity; no individual entries of A are needed. The dimension enters through trace, not determinant.
Why not the others: (A) reports the scalar alone; (B) assumes two dimensions; (C) drops the negative sign.
Key point: Apply the adjugate identity before taking trace.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Events A and B are independent with P(A)=1/2 and P(B)=1/3. What is P(A∪B)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2/3.
Given: Independent events can overlap.
Formula/Principle: P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B); union subtracts intersection once.
Step 1: Intersection=1/6; union=1/2+1/3−1/6=2/3.
Worked derivation: \[P(A\cup B)=\frac12+\frac13-\left(\frac12\right)\left(\frac13\right)=\frac23.\]
Why: Independence supplies a nonzero overlap, unlike mutual exclusivity. Adding probabilities without subtracting overlap counts outcomes in both events twice. Their intersection is exactly the product of the two nonzero event probabilities under the given independence condition.
Why not the others: (B) omits overlap correction; (C) gives intersection only; (D) reports P(A).
Key point: Independent and mutually exclusive are different relations.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Five distinct people sit at a round table; rotations count as the same arrangement. How many arrangements have A and B not adjacent?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 12.
Given: Rotational symmetry but reflections remain distinct.
Formula/Principle: Total (5−1)!; adjacent pair as a block 2!(4−1)!.
Step 1: 24−12=12.
Worked derivation: \[N=(5-1)!-2(4-1)!=24-12=12.\]
Why: Fixing one person's position removes rotation. Counting an AB block in both orders captures every forbidden adjacency exactly once for five distinct people.
Why not the others: (A) halves for reflections incorrectly; (C) subtracts too few forbidden cases; (D) includes adjacent pairs.
Key point: Use a block for circular adjacency, then complement.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Find the coefficient of x³ in (1−2x)⁶.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −160.
Given: Term with x³ chooses three factors of −2x.
Formula/Principle: Coefficient=C(6,3)(−2)³.
Step 1: 20×(−8)=−160.
Worked derivation: \[[x^3](1-2x)^6=\binom63(-2)^3=20(-8)=-160.\]
Why: The odd power preserves the negative sign, and the factor 2 must itself be cubed. The binomial coefficient alone counts choices, not their product weight.
Why not the others: (A) loses sign; (B) misses a factor two; (D) omits the cube of two.
Key point: Include both combinatorial count and signed term value.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let \(S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}1/[n(n+1)(n+2)]\). What is the least positive integer N for which S_N>1/5?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) N=2.
Given: Three consecutive factors and a strict threshold for the partial sum.
Formula/Principle: 1/[n(n+1)(n+2)]=(1/2)[1/(n(n+1))−1/((n+1)(n+2))].
Step 1: S_N=1/4−1/[2(N+1)(N+2)].
Step 2: S_N>1/5 requires (N+1)(N+2)>10, first true at N=2.
Worked derivation: \[\frac14-\frac1{2(N+1)(N+2)}>\frac15\iff (N+1)(N+2)>10;\quad N_{\min}=2.\]
Why: The rational blocks telescope to a formula retaining a positive endpoint correction. The strict inequality rejects N=1 because (2)(3)=6, while N=2 has (3)(4)=12; the question asks the first crossing, not the sum at a fixed ten terms.
Why not the others: (A) gives S₁=1/6 below 1/5; (B) works but is not least; (C) also works but is not least.
Key point: Derive the finite remainder, then solve the threshold inequality.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For real a, define \(L(a)=\lim_{x\to0}(|x-a|-|a|)/x\), if a finite two-sided limit exists. Which statement is complete?
options: A) It exists for all a≠0 and equals −sgn(a); at a=0 it fails
B) It exists for all a and equals 0
C) It exists only for a=0 and equals 1
D) It exists for all a>0 and nowhere else
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Exists exactly when a≠0.
Given: Absolute value has different local branches depending on sign of a and x.
Formula/Principle: Evaluate the local expression separately for a>0, a<0 and a=0.
Step 1: For a>0 and |x| small, |x−a|=a−x gives −1; for a<0, |x−a|=x−a gives +1.
Worked derivation: \[L(a)=\begin{cases}-1,&a>0,\\+1,&a<0,\end{cases}\qquad L(0)=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{|x|}{x}\ \text{does not exist}.\]
Why: At zero the quotient is +1 from the right and −1 from the left, so no two-sided value exists. Away from zero the inside of the absolute value retains one sign locally, giving a standard derivative.
Why not the others: (B) ignores branch slopes; (C) gives a one-sided value at zero; (D) excludes valid negative a.
Key point: Test the cusp parameter separately from smooth branches.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A quantity y(t)>0 follows dy/dt=2ty and starts at y(0)=3. What is its value at t=1?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 3e.
Given: Separable first-order IVP.
Formula/Principle: dy/y=2t dt, then use the initial value.
Step 1: ln y=t²+C; y(0)=3 fixes e^C=3.
Worked derivation: \[y(t)=3e^{t^2},\qquad y(1)=3e.\]
Why: Integrating 2t produces t², not 2t²; the multiplicative constant survives the exponential and is fixed by y(0). The selected expression follows only after both the integration and initial condition.
Why not the others: (A) omits initial factor; (C) uses an incorrect exponent; (D) treats the exponential as a linear factor.
Key point: Apply the initial condition after integration.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The lines L₁: (x,y,z)=(t,0,0) and L₂: (x,y,z)=(0,1+s,1) extend indefinitely. What is their shortest distance?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.
Given: L₁ lies in z=0 and L₂ in z=1; their xy projections cross at (0,0).
Formula/Principle: Any joining vector has vertical component 1, hence length ≥1; attain equality when xy coordinates coincide.
Step 1: Choose t=0, s=−1, giving points (0,0,0) and (0,0,1).
Worked derivation: \[d_{\min}=\|(0,0,1)-(0,0,0)\|=1.\]
Why: The two lines are skew but their projections meet, so a vertical common perpendicular achieves the lower bound imposed by z separation. An arbitrary pair of points gives a longer segment.
Why not the others: (A) requires intersecting z levels; (B) includes an avoidable horizontal offset; (D) doubles the vertical gap.
Key point: Prove both a distance lower bound and an attaining pair.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For vectors a=(1,1,0), b=(0,1,1), c=(1,0,k), what k makes a,b,c coplanar?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) −1.
Given: Coplanarity means scalar triple product zero.
Formula/Principle: (a×b)·c=0.
Step 1: a×b=(1,−1,1), so dot with c gives 1+k.
Worked derivation: \[(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)\cdot\mathbf c=(1,-1,1)\cdot(1,0,k)=1+k=0\Rightarrow k=-1.\]
Why: The scalar triple product is the signed volume of the vectors' parallelepiped. Vanishing volume means linear dependence and thus a common plane through the origin.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the needed sign; (B) leaves volume one; (C) yields negative volume.
Key point: Set the triple product to zero rather than its magnitude to one.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Values 1,2,4 have frequencies 1,2,1. Find the mean absolute deviation from their arithmetic mean.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 7/8.
Given: Four observations counted with multiplicity.
Formula/Principle: Mean=Σfx/Σf; mean deviation=Σf|x−mean|/Σf.
Step 1: Mean=(1+4+4)/4=9/4.
Worked derivation: \[\mathrm{MD}=\frac{|1-9/4|+2|2-9/4|+|4-9/4|}{4}=\frac{5/4+2/4+7/4}{4}=\frac78.\]
Why: Frequencies weight both the mean and absolute deviations. Squaring instead of taking absolute values would calculate a variance-like quantity rather than the statistic requested.
Why not the others: (B) ignores one deviation; (C) uses an unweighted average; (D) reports the mean.
Key point: Use the same frequency weights at both steps.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Using principal ranges arcsin∈[−π/2,π/2], arccos∈[0,π], arctan∈(−π/2,π/2), evaluate arcsin(sin 7π/6)+arccos(cos 7π/6)+arctan(tan 7π/6).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 5π/6.
Given: 7π/6 lies in quadrant III; each inverse function has a different principal range.
Formula/Principle: Reduce each periodic angle into its own inverse-function branch.
Step 1: arcsin(sin7π/6)=−π/6; arccos(cos7π/6)=5π/6; arctan(tan7π/6)=π/6.
Worked derivation: \[-\frac\pi6+\frac{5\pi}6+\frac\pi6=\frac{5\pi}6.\]
Why: The inverse of a periodic trigonometric function returns its principal representative, not necessarily the original angle. Sine, cosine and tangent use distinct ranges, so reducing them with one common offset gives the wrong total.
Why not the others: (A) drops one branch term; (C) keeps an unreduced angle; (D) mishandles the tangent branch.
Key point: Reduce every inverse trigonometric term independently.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A 2 kg block rests on the floor of a lift accelerating upward at 2 m s⁻². With g=10 m s⁻², what normal force does the floor exert?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 24 N.
Given: Lift and block accelerate upward together.
Formula/Principle: N−mg=ma.
Step 1: N=m(g+a)=2(10+2)=24 N.
Worked derivation: \[N-mg=ma\quad\Rightarrow\quad N=2(10+2)=24\,\mathrm N.\]
Why: Upward acceleration requires an upward net force, so the floor's normal must exceed weight. The block is stationary relative to the cabin but accelerated in the ground frame.
Why not the others: (A) assumes downward acceleration; (B) uses weight alone; (D) adds the acceleration twice.
Key point: Choose a frame and apply Newton's second law consistently.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A 1 kg block starts from rest 2 m above a horizontal rough track. After descending a smooth ramp, it travels 3 m across a rough stretch with μ=0.20, then compresses a spring of k=100 N m⁻¹ on the same rough surface. With g=10 m s⁻², which equation and approximate maximum compression x are correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Equation including friction through compression.
Given: Initial gravitational energy 20 J; rough approach loss μmg(3)=6 J; friction over spring displacement is μmgx=2x J.
Formula/Principle: Remaining energy=elastic storage+additional friction.
Step 1: 20=6+2x+½(100)x², so 50x²+2x−14=0.
Worked derivation: \[x=\frac{-2+\sqrt{2^2+4(50)(14)}}{100}=\frac{\sqrt{701}-1}{50}\approx0.510\,\mathrm m.\]
Why: Friction removes energy both before and during spring compression because the spring is on the same rough surface. The positive quadratic root gives physical compression; the negative root is rejected.
Why not the others: (A) ignores all friction; (B) ignores friction during compression; (C) applies the approach loss as a coefficient of x.
Key point: Account for dissipative work over every rough distance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Inside a uniform-density planet of radius R, gravitational acceleration at distance R/3 from the centre is what fraction of surface g?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) One third.
Given: Spherical uniform density; interior enclosed mass scales as r³.
Formula/Principle: g(r)=GM(r)/r², with M(r)=M(r/R)³.
Step 1: g(r)/g(R)=r/R; at r=R/3 the ratio is 1/3.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{g(R/3)}{g(R)}=\frac{M(R/3)/(R/3)^2}{M/R^2}=\frac{(1/3)^3}{(1/3)^2}=\frac13.\]
Why: Using the entire planet mass at an interior point would be wrong: outer spherical shells contribute no net field there. Only the enclosed mass shrinks with radius, leaving a linear dependence.
Why not the others: (B) uses inverse-square distance with fixed mass; (C) assumes surface field throughout; (D) reverses the linear ratio.
Key point: Apply the shell theorem before Newton's inverse-square law.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Read the two-regime stress–strain plot. Which elastic modulus follows from the initial straight segment?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 50 GPa.
Given: Elastic endpoint stress 100×10⁶ Pa, strain 0.002.
Formula/Principle: Young modulus is slope dσ/dε in the elastic segment.
Step 1: 100×10⁶/0.002=50×10⁹ Pa.
Worked derivation: \[Y=\frac{\Delta\sigma}{\Delta\varepsilon}=\frac{100\,\mathrm{MPa}}{0.002}=50000\,\mathrm{MPa}=50\,\mathrm{GPa}.\]
Why: A later plastic slope does not represent Young modulus of the initial reversible response. Strain is dimensionless, so the ratio has pressure units.
Why not the others: (A) divides by an incorrect strain; (C) uses the numerical stress as modulus; (D) applies a factor four.
Key point: Read slope only from the elastic part of the graph.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A 100 g ice sample at 0°C is mixed in an insulated vessel with 100 g water at 50°C. Take water c=4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and ice latent heat L=334 J g⁻¹. What is the final state?
options: A) All ice melts and water reaches 5°C
C) About 63 g ice melts; mixture remains at 0°C
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) About 63 g melts at 0°C.
Given: Water can release 100×4.2×50=21000 J cooling to zero; melting all ice needs 33400 J.
Formula/Principle: At phase plateau, available heat melts mass m=Q/L.
Step 1: 21000/334≈62.9 g, leaving about 37.1 g ice.
Worked derivation: \[m_{\rm melted}=\frac{(100)(4.2)(50)}{334}\approx62.9\,\mathrm g<100\,\mathrm g.\]
Why: The warm water runs out of sensible heat before all ice melts. Coexisting ice and water fix final equilibrium at 0°C under the stated pressure assumption.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) require more melting heat than available; (D) ignores the positive heat transfer.
Key point: Test whether the phase change completes before solving for final temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: An ideal-gas mixture contains equal numbers of molecules of gases X and Y at a common temperature; their molar masses are 4 and 16 units. If vY is the rms speed of species Y, what is the rms speed computed over all molecules in the mixture divided by vY?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) √(5/2).
Given: Equal molecule counts, common temperature, and masses MX:MY=4:16.
Formula/Principle: Species mean-square speeds scale as 1/M; the pooled mean square is the count-weighted average.
Step 1: ⟨vX²⟩/⟨vY²⟩=MY/MX=4.
Step 2: ⟨v²⟩mix/⟨vY²⟩=(4+1)/2=5/2.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{v_{\rm rms,mix}}{v_Y}=\sqrt{\frac{\langle v_X^2\rangle+\langle v_Y^2\rangle}{2\langle v_Y^2\rangle}}=\sqrt{\frac{4+1}{2}}=\sqrt{\frac52}.\]
Why: rms means square first, average across all molecules, then take the square root. Averaging the two rms speeds directly would be mathematically different; equal mole fractions justify equal weights.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the mass trend; (B) discards X's larger speeds; (C) uses an incorrect weighted square.
Key point: Combine mean-square speeds before taking the mixture rms.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The figure specifies pendulum P in a lab and Q in an upward-accelerating lift, including their lengths and effective acceleration. For small oscillations, what is TQ/TP?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) One half.
Given: P experiences g; Q has effective g'=g+g=2g and length L/2.
Formula/Principle: T=2π√(length/effective gravity).
Step 1: TQ/TP=√[(L/2)/(2g) ÷ (L/g)]=√(1/4)=1/2.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{T_Q}{T_P}=\sqrt{\frac{(L/2)/(2g)}{L/g}}=\frac12.\]
Why: Both a shorter pendulum and stronger effective gravity shorten Q's period. Applying only one change gives 1/√2 instead of the combined factor. The effective gravity in the accelerating cabin is upward acceleration plus ordinary g, while the string length is separately halved.
Why not the others: (B) uses only one change; (C) assumes the effects cancel; (D) reverses the combined effect.
Key point: Put both changes inside the period square root.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Capacitors C and 2C are in series across an ideal battery V. While the battery remains connected, dielectric of κ=2 completely fills the C capacitor. What is the ratio of the new series charge to the original series charge?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 3/2.
Given: Initially C and 2C in series; after insertion they are 2C and 2C in series with fixed battery V.
Formula/Principle: Q=CeqV for each state.
Step 1: Ceq,old=2C/3; Ceq,new=C.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{Q_{\rm new}}{Q_{\rm old}}=\frac{C V}{(2C/3)V}=\frac32.\]
Why: The connected battery supplies additional free charge as total capacitance increases. Treating the original series charge as fixed would apply a disconnected-circuit condition instead.
Why not the others: (A) ignores dielectric insertion; (C) reverses the ratio; (D) uses capacitance of one plate pair as the initial equivalent.
Key point: A connected ideal battery fixes voltage across the series combination.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Moving Charges and Magnetism / Magnetism and Matter
questions.question: A magnetic dipole of magnitude m is in uniform B. Its orientation changes from parallel to perpendicular to B. What change in potential energy occurs?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) +mB.
Given: θ changes from 0 to π/2.
Formula/Principle: U=−mB cosθ.
Step 1: Uinitial=−mB, Ufinal=0; ΔU=+mB.
Worked derivation: \[\Delta U=-mB\cos(\pi/2)-[-mB\cos0]=0+mB=mB.\]
Why: Parallel orientation is lowest energy, and rotating against the aligning tendency raises potential energy. The sign belongs to final minus initial, not the torque direction.
Why not the others: (A) reverses endpoints; (B) omits orientation dependence; (D) uses an antiparallel final state.
Key point: Evaluate both orientation energies before subtracting.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.question: A permanent electric dipole p in uniform E is initially perpendicular to the field and rotates into alignment without friction. How do its torque magnitude and potential energy change between these endpoints?
options: B) Torque stays maximum; energy decreases
C) Torque falls to zero; energy increases
D) Torque falls to zero; energy decreases
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Torque zero, energy lower.
Why: Torque magnitude is pE sinθ, largest at 90° and zero at alignment. Potential U=−pE cosθ falls from zero to −pE, with the released energy available for rotation.
Why not the others: (A) reverses both trends; (B) retains nonzero aligned torque; (C) gives the wrong energy sign.
Worked derivation: \[\tau_i=pE,\ \tau_f=0;\qquad U_i=0,\ U_f=-pE.\]
Key point: Torque and potential have different angular functions.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A Wheatstone bridge has left arms 2 Ω and 3 Ω and right upper arm 4 Ω; the right lower arm is a 5 Ω resistor at 0°C with temperature coefficient 0.004 °C⁻¹. At what temperature is the bridge balanced?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 50°C.
Given: Balance ratio 2/3=4/R; R(T)=5(1+0.004T).
Formula/Principle: Solve bridge balance, then temperature-resistance relation.
Step 1: R=6 Ω; 6/5−1=0.2=0.004T.
Worked derivation: \[\frac23=\frac4R\Rightarrow R=6\,\Omega;\quad 6=5(1+0.004T)\Rightarrow T=50^\circ\mathrm C.\]
Why: At balance the bridge detector current vanishes, setting arm ratios. Heating raises the lower-right resistance from five to six ohms; solving the material law afterwards avoids mixing circuit and temperature effects.
Why not the others: (B) yields 5.5 Ω; (C) yields 6.5 Ω; (D) yields 7 Ω.
Key point: Solve the electrical target resistance first.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Using the indices and incoming angle in the parallel-layer diagram, what happens to the ray at the final layer–air interface?
options: A) Total internal reflection before reaching B
B) It emerges grazing the air surface
C) It emerges into air at 30°
D) It refracts into air at 45°
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Grazing emergence.
Given: Parallel interfaces; nA sin30°=2×1/2=1.
Formula/Principle: Snell's law keeps n sinθ constant through parallel layers.
Step 1: In B, sinθB=1/√2, θB=45°; in air, sinθair=1, θair=90°.
Worked derivation: \[2\sin30^\circ=\sqrt2\sin45^\circ=1\sin90^\circ=1.\]
Why: The ray reaches the critical angle at the last interface, so transmitted direction lies along the boundary in the ideal geometric limit. It is not beyond critical, so ordinary total internal reflection is not the correct description.
Why not the others: (A) ignores transmission into B; (C) carries the original angle without Snell correction; (D) copies the B angle into air.
Key point: Propagate the conserved n sinθ across both boundaries.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: From the stopping-potential plot for a metal, infer its work function in electronvolts.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2 eV.
Given: Graph slope (1 V)/(2.5×10¹⁴ Hz)=4×10⁻¹⁵ V s, equal to h/e.
Formula/Principle: Threshold hf₀=φ; in eV, φ/e=(h/e)f₀.
Step 1: (4×10⁻¹⁵)(5×10¹⁴)=2 V numerically, hence 2 eV.
Worked derivation: \[\frac\phi e=\frac he f_0=\frac{1\,\mathrm V}{(7.5-5)\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}}(5\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz})=2\,\mathrm V.\]
Why: The graph's zero intercept supplies threshold frequency and its slope supplies Planck's constant per electron charge. Both are needed; a stopping potential of one volt at one frequency is not the work function.
Why not the others: (A) uses a wrong frequency ratio; (B) copies the plotted voltage; (D) doubles the slope result.
Key point: Read slope and threshold separately from a photoelectric graph.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The hydrogen-level figure shows a direct 4→2 emission A and a two-step cascade 4→3→2 with photons B and C. What are the ratios (energy B+C)/(energy A) and (number of photons in cascade)/(number in direct path)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Energy ratio 1; photon-count ratio 2.
Given: Both paths start at n=4 and end at n=2.
Formula/Principle: Photon energies equal positive differences of the hydrogen level energies.
Step 1: EB=E4−E3, EC=E3−E2, and EA=E4−E2 when levels are measured as positive emitted differences.
Worked derivation: \[E_B+E_C=(E_4-E_3)+(E_3-E_2)=E_4-E_2=E_A;\qquad \frac{N_{\rm cascade}}{N_{\rm direct}}=\frac21=2.\]
Why: The intermediate n=3 energy cancels in the total: two smaller photons can carry the same total energy as one direct photon. Energy conservation fixes the first ratio, while counting the arrows fixes the second; the individual photon wavelengths need not match.
Why not the others: (A) doubles energy as well as photon count; (B) halves the conserved total; (C) ignores the extra emitted photon.
Key point: Sum transition energies over a cascade, then count photons.
questions.image_alt: Hydrogen energy levels and two transitions

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A conducting rod of length 1.0 m rotates about one end at 10 rad s⁻¹ in a perpendicular uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. What emf develops between its ends?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1.0 V.
Given: Rod length 1 m, angular speed 10 rad s⁻¹, field 0.20 T.
Formula/Principle: Element at radius r has speed ωr and incremental emf dε=Bωr dr.
Step 1: Integrate from pivot 0 to L: ε=½BωL².
Worked derivation: \[\varepsilon=\int_0^L B\omega r\,dr=\frac12(0.20)(10)(1)^2=1.0\,\mathrm V.\]
Why: Speed increases along the rod, so replacing all elements by tip speed overestimates emf by a factor two. The perpendicular field makes the radial motional-force component maximal.
Why not the others: (B) uses tip speed everywhere; (C) omits angular speed; (D) omits both the half and B.
Key point: Integrate local motional emf over a rotating rod.
